Notes: 139 BCE (consuls M. Popilius Laenas and L. Calpurnius): the praetor peregrinus Cn. Cornelius Hispalus expelled the Chaldeans and also the Judeans, who had tried to pass their sacred rites to Romans (cult of "Jupiter Sabazius" per the Paris epitome), and abolished their private and public altars; Valerius Maximus 1.3.3 known only through the epitomes of Nepotianus and Julius Paris. Earliest documented Jewish residents in Rome = basis of Year Established. Small community; the expulsion was temporary and sporadic and its historicity is debated by some scholars (Harland). Population blank, not 0: no source says no Jews remained.

61 BCE: Jewish prisoners brought to Rome by Pompey after his campaigns in Judea (Jerusalem taken 63 BCE; triumph 61 BCE) joined the existing Jews of Rome (Encyclopaedia Judaica, "Rome"). Captives; number not given. Event that greatly enlarged the community (most Roman Jews later were freedmen descended from such captives).

59 BCE: Cicero, Pro Flacco 28.66-67, speaking near the Aurelian steps, refers to "the multitude of Jews, which at times was most unruly in the assemblies" and to gold "exported out of Italy" every year for the Jews (Temple tax to Jerusalem). Earliest secure literary evidence of a substantial, politically visible Jewish community in Rome; no number given.

Monteverde Jewish catacomb (Via Portuense): H. J. Leon assigned a possible 1st-century BCE date to its original use by Jews (1st c. BCE = -50, c.), the earliest date proposed for any Jewish catacomb in Rome; however brick stamps begin only under Augustus (Rutgers) and Noy/Ferrua date the securely provenanced inscriptions mainly to the 3rd-4th c. CE. Weak/disputed archaeological indication of a Jewish burial ground in this period.

Caesar exempted the Jewish synagogues from the laws he enacted to curb the power of the Roman collegia (Encyclopaedia Judaica, "Rome"). Undated in the source; placed at the midpoint of Caesar's dictatorship (49-44 BCE), c. Implies organized Jewish congregations in Rome.

44 BCE: at Julius Caesar's funeral a multitude of foreigners mourned "but especially the Jews, who for several nights together frequented the spot where the body was burnt" (Suetonius, Divus Julius 84). Literary attestation of a resident Jewish community; no number.

Augustan period (27 BCE-14 CE, midpoint c. -6): Philo, Legatio ad Gaium 155-157: Augustus knew that "the great division of Rome which is on the other side of the river Tiber" (Trastevere) was inhabited by Jews, "mostly Roman citizens, having been emancipated" after being brought to Italy as captives; they had houses of prayer (synagogues), met on the sabbath and sent first-fruit money to Jerusalem. A large, organized community concentrated in Trastevere; no number.

Augustan period (27 BCE-14 CE, midpoint c. -6): "Only with Augustus is there clear-cut evidence of an organized Jewish community in Rome"; "At least three synagogues can be dated to the Augustan period" (from synagogue names in later catacomb inscriptions, e.g. Augustesians, Agrippesians) (Encyclopaedia Judaica, "Rome"). Several congregations imply a community of many thousands; no number given for this period (EJ's figure of c. 10,000 refers to late imperial Rome and is outside this period).

Estimate of A. Hausrath (Neutestamentliche Zeitgeschichte III, p. 384), as cited by Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church I, n. 486: "40,000 Jews in Rome under Augustus". Dated to midpoint of Augustus' reign (27 BCE-14 CE), c. Schaff notes Josephus' data "do not justify a very definite calculation".

4 BCE: Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1 (17.300): the 50 ambassadors of the Judean nation who came to Augustus against Archelaus were joined by "above eight thousand of the Jews that were at Rome already". The 8,000 are a subset (adult men who joined a demonstration / crowd figure), not the whole community; ancient figure. Modern writers multiply it by c. 5 to get c. 40,000 (see following rows).

Modern estimate (Livius.org article "Jewish Rome"): under Augustus "there must have been some 40,000 Jews" in Rome, derived by multiplying Josephus' 8,000 adult men who sided with the Judean embassy of 4 BCE by a nuclear family of at least four or five. Author adds the number likely rose after the mass deportation of prisoners of war after 70 CE.

Estimate by Peter Eyland (non-peer-reviewed ancient history website, 2004): "a population of about 40,000 Jews (i.e. ~4% of the total population) seems a reasonable guess", derived from Josephus' 8,000 of 4 BCE (treated as indicative of a large crowd); he notes Barclay (1996: 295 n. 32) cites three scholarly estimates ranging from 20,000 to 60,000, and that the 4,000 conscripted in 19 CE are consistent with c. 40,000.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), "Rome": "a reasonable estimate of the number of Jews in Rome during the empire would give at least 40,000". The estimate is for the imperial period generally (undated); placed at the brief's early-Roman midpoint (63 BCE-70 CE = 4), c. JE also states that until the 1st century CE the Jewish settlement occupied Trastevere and that synagogues existed as early as Augustus. [Review fix: Population 40000 moved to Notes; the source gives no date ("during the empire", i.e. any time over five centuries), so it cannot be placed in the Second Temple period]

19 CE: Josephus, Antiquities 18.3.5 (18.81-84): after four Jewish swindlers defrauded the proselyte Fulvia, Tiberius "ordered all the Jews to be banished out of Rome; at which time the consuls listed four thousand men out of them" and "sent them to the island Sardinia". The 4,000 are a subset (conscripted men), not the community. Population blank, not 0: scholars regard the expulsion as partial and temporary.

19 CE expulsion: Tacitus, Annals 2.85: "four thousand men libertini generis were sent to Sardinia to help suppress brigandage there" (adherents of Egyptian and Jewish rites); Cassius Dio says the Jews "had flocked to Rome in great numbers". L. V. Rutgers (Classical Antiquity 13, 1994) argues the measure "could not have encompassed all Jewish citizens living Rome at this time" and that "exact figures, however, cannot be given". 4,000 = subset of freedmen, not the community size.

Estimate of A. Hausrath (Neutestamentliche Zeitgeschichte III, p. 384), as cited by Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church I, n. 486: "60,000 under Tiberius". Dated to midpoint of Tiberius' reign (14-37 CE), c. Schaff regards Josephus' data as insufficient for a definite calculation.
After the death of Sejanus (31 CE) Tiberius allowed the Jews to return to Rome (Jewish Encyclopedia 1906, "Rome"). End of the 19 CE banishment; community re-established.

c. 41 CE: Cassius Dio (60.6.6), as quoted by L. V. Rutgers (1994): "Claudius did not banish the Jews from Rome, because there were too many of them". Dio places this at the start of Claudius' reign (41 CE); date from Dio's narrative context, c. Indicates a very large community, no number. Rutgers argues Jews were expelled only once under Claudius (contra Smallwood's two measures).

Claudius' expulsion: Suetonius, Divus Claudius 25.4: "Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome." Date c. 49 CE from Orosius 7.6.15 (ninth year of Claudius), not stated by Suetonius; date debated (41 vs 49). Population blank, not 0: the expulsion was partial/temporary (cf. Dio).

c. 49-50 CE: Acts 18:2: Paul met at Corinth "a Jew named Aquila from Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome". Named Jewish residents of Rome (expelled). Population blank, not 0: modern scholars (e.g. Rutgers, Dio) hold that not all Jews left and the measure was temporary.

Estimate cited by Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church I (main text, citing Renan, Friedländer and Harnack): the Jews of Rome in the apostolic age "estimated at twenty or thirty thousand souls"; midpoint of the range 20,000-30,000. Apostolic age dated c. 50 CE (1st c. CE midpoint). Schaff adds they lived mostly in Trastevere and were mainly descendants of slaves and captives of Pompey, Cassius and Antony.

c. 60 CE: Acts 28:17: three days after arriving in Rome, Paul "called together the local leaders of the Jews" (rulers of the synagogues). Literary attestation of an organized community with several synagogue leaders, re-established after the Claudian expulsion; no number.

c. 63/64 CE (Josephus' 26th year): Josephus, Life 3 (13-16) on his voyage to Rome: he became acquainted with "Aliturius, an actor of plays, and much beloved by Nero, but a Jew by birth", through whom he met the empress Poppaea and obtained the release of priests sent to Rome by Felix. Named Jewish individual resident in Rome.

71 CE: Josephus, War 7.5.3 (7.116-118): Titus ordered "the leaders of the captives, Simon and John, with the other seven hundred men" to be carried to Italy to be produced in his triumph (held in Rome 71 CE). Captives, not residents; the community grew afterwards from enslaved war captives (cf. Livius, EJ). Population blank.

c. 71 CE: Josephus, Life 422-423: after sailing to Rome with Titus, Vespasian "gave me an apartment in his own house" and Roman citizenship and an annual pension. Named Jewish individual (Josephus) resident in Rome from 71 CE.
